sections.h2: How does an Indiana sheriff sale work?
sections.html:
An Indiana sheriff sale is the public auction that follows a court judgment of foreclosure, and the county sheriff runs it. Because Indiana foreclosures go through a judge, the sale comes late in a chain of notices, filings and waiting periods.

The sale rules sit in IC 32-29-7. The sheriff has to sell the property in a way "reasonably likely to bring the highest net proceeds" after expenses, and a judge can order an auctioneer when a sale that way is economically feasible or when all creditors agree to it. If an auctioneer is used, the sheriff must engage one within 14 days of the order.

Sales may take place between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. on any day except Sunday, and the sheriff may hold them electronically, at the sheriff's office, or at another location likely to attract higher bids.

sections.h2: What is the timeline from missed payments to the sale?
sections.html:
The statutes put minimum gaps between each step, and the table shows the ones that apply to a typical owner-occupied home.

StepTimingStatute
Presuit notice by certified mailAt least 30 days before the lender filesIC 32-30-10.5-8
Request a settlement conferenceWithin 30 days after the complaint is servedIC 32-30-10.5-8
Process on a judgment may issueNot until 3 months after the complaint is filedIC 32-29-7-3
Lender files the praecipeGenerally within 180 daysIC 32-29-7-3
Sheriff schedules the saleWithin 120 days after certification (60 days for judgments on abandoned property)IC 32-29-7-3
Newspaper noticeOnce a week for 3 weeks; first notice at least 30 days before the saleIC 32-29-7-3

The lender pays an administrative fee of up to $300 when it files the praecipe. At the first publication the sheriff also serves written notice on each owner, and the fee for that service is $10 for one owner and $3 for each additional one. Notices also go up at the courthouse door. If the sale is canceled, the sheriff has to notify each owner in writing.

sections.h2: What can a homeowner do before the sheriff sale?
sections.html:
The owner has several options before the auction, from a settlement conference to paying the judgment.

  • Request a settlement conference. For an owner-occupied home, the court mails a notice of the right to one, and the owner must ask within 30 days after service of the complaint. The Indiana Attorney General's page says that if the owner requests a conference, the judge cannot sign the foreclosure order until it has taken place, and the lender must send a representative.
  • Call the foreclosure hotline. The Indiana Foreclosure Prevention Network can be reached at 877-438-4673 (877-GET-HOPE), and it can connect a homeowner with a pro bono attorney for the conference.
  • Redeem before the sale. Under IC 32-29-7-7, any owner or part owner can pay the judgment plus interest and costs before the sale. The money goes to the clerk if the decree has not yet been issued to the sheriff, and to the sheriff after that. Once the property is redeemed, the sale cannot proceed and the order of sale is vacated.
  • Stay put. IC 32-29-7-11 lets an owner who lives in the property keep possession rent free until the foreclosure sale, provided the court finds no waste or damage. An owner who stops paying taxes may keep only the part used as a dwelling, up to fifteen acres.

A part owner who redeems gets a lien on the other owners' shares for their portion, bearing 8 percent annual interest plus costs. That rule matters for heirs who share a house and are not all on the same page about paying.

The details vary by county, but a good example is the Grant County Sheriff's page. Sales there are held at 10:00 a.m. at the Sheriff's Department in Marion, bidders must submit a handwritten bid form before that hour, and there is no minimum bid.

The winning bidder must pay in full by 3:00 p.m. that day, or the sale is voided and the next highest bidder is notified. The dollar figure on the sale list is the judgment owed when the paperwork was filed. It is not necessarily what the bank will bid, and the bank is always represented by fax or in person. The office says it has no keys, does not show properties and has no information about them, and it adds that if a house is occupied the sheriff will evict the occupants within 24 hours.

Bidders face a legal check as well. IC 32-29-7-4.6, added by a 2022 law, requires each bidder to sign a sworn statement that they owe no delinquent property taxes, no unpaid judgments to a local government and no building code penalties, and that they are not bidding for someone barred from the sale. Giving false information is a Level 6 felony. IC 32-29-7-9 also bars the sheriff from buying at the sale.

sections.h2: What taxes and liens must be paid before the sale?
sections.html: The side that asked for the sale has to pay delinquent real estate taxes first. Under IC 32-29-7-8.5, the party that filed the praecipe must pay delinquent property taxes, sewer liens, special assessments, penalties and interest due on the sale date, or the amount needed to redeem if a tax sale certificate is outstanding. If those payments are not made in full by the sale date, the sheriff must cancel the sale, and a new sale needs a fresh praecipe, costs, and re-advertising.

sections.h2: What does the buyer receive, and what happens to leftover money?
sections.html:
The sheriff prepares a deed and delivers it to the buyer right after the sale, and files it with the county recorder unless the foreclosed mortgage was HUD-insured. The deed has to be sufficient to pass the full interest of every party to the suit and anyone claiming under them. The sheriff then files a return with the clerk.

The sale money follows a set order under IC 32-30-10-14. First come the expenses of the offer and sale, then principal, interest and costs, then the remaining secured balance not yet due. If anything is left, it goes to the clerk, and the court directs it to the mortgage debtor, the debtor's heirs, or others the debtor assigned to.

Allen County has put numbers on this. A court program launched in 2021 found 45 former owners with a combined $282,000 in unclaimed surplus, and the individual amounts ranged from under $200 to nearly $50,000. Claims are made by letter to the clerk with the original case number, a court order is needed to release the money, and unclaimed funds can move to the Indiana Attorney General's Unclaimed Property Division after five years.

sections.h2: How is a sheriff sale different from a tax sale?
sections.html:
A sheriff sale enforces a mortgage lender's judgment, while a tax sale collects delinquent property taxes through the county treasurer. They can overlap on the same house, since the party seeking a sheriff sale must clear delinquent taxes before the auction.

  • The sheriff conducts a sheriff sale after a court judgment. The county treasurer conducts a tax sale of delinquent parcels.
  • A mortgage foreclosure gives the owner redemption before the sale, and section 13 of the chapter excludes other means of redemption. A tax sale generally leaves a one year redemption period afterward.
  • A sheriff sale produces a sheriff's deed. A tax sale produces a certificate first, and a tax deed only after the redemption period and a court process.

sections.h2: What should a seller expect when selling before an Indiana sheriff sale?
sections.html:
An owner who sells before the auction still has to clear the lien, so the closing figure includes the lender's payoff. Redemption under IC 32-29-7-7 requires paying the judgment, interest and costs, and the exact payoff has to come from the lender's side.

Sellers in this spot are often dealing with a vacant or damaged house, back taxes and tenants or relatives who have stopped paying. A cash purchase as-is can fit that situation, but the closing has to be completed before the sale date, so the court calendar sets the timeline.

faqs.q: How long after foreclosure is filed does an Indiana sheriff sale happen?
faqs.a: Process on the judgment cannot issue until three months after the complaint is filed. After that, the lender files a praecipe, and the sheriff must schedule the sale within 120 days of certification, with three weeks of newspaper notice. In practice, the total depends on the county and on any settlement conference.

faqs.q: Can I stop an Indiana sheriff sale?
faqs.a: You can redeem before the sale by paying the judgment, interest and costs under IC 32-29-7-7. You can also request a settlement conference within 30 days of service, and a sale is canceled if the party who requested it has not paid the delinquent taxes.

faqs.q: Do I have to leave my house before the sheriff sale?
faqs.a: No. IC 32-29-7-11 lets an owner keep possession of a home used as a dwelling until the sale, rent free, as long as the court finds no waste or damage. The statute does not extend that right past the sale.

faqs.q: What happens to extra money from an Indiana sheriff sale?
faqs.a: Any surplus after expenses, principal, interest and costs goes to the clerk of the court, who pays it to the mortgage debtor, heirs or assignees on court order. Allen County's program shows surplus amounts from under $200 to nearly $50,000.

faqs.q: Is there a minimum bid at an Indiana sheriff sale?
faqs.a: The statute sets none in the sections reviewed, and Grant County's sheriff says there is no minimum bid. The amount on the sale list is the judgment, and the lender's own bid may differ.

faqs.q: Who can bid at an Indiana sheriff sale?
faqs.a: Any bidder who can sign the sworn statement under IC 32-29-7-4.6, which covers delinquent taxes, local government judgments and building code penalties. The sheriff cannot buy at the sale.
